name: GGUF Q8_0
bpw_note: approx.; 8.5008 measured on Llama-3.1-8B (llama.cpp quantize README); nominal 8.5 = 32 int8 values + one FP16 scale per block
best_for: A near-lossless reference copy at roughly half the size of FP16.
how: Weights are split into blocks of 32, and each block stores 32 signed 8-bit integers plus one FP16 scale. A weight is rebuilt by multiplying its integer by the block scale; llama.cpp ignores an importance matrix for this type.

name: GGUF Q6_K
bpw_note: approx.; 6.5633 measured on Llama-3.1-8B; nominal 6.5625 for the Q6_K block itself
best_for: Quality-first local inference that still saves about a fifth of the memory of Q8_0.
how: Weights are grouped into 256-weight super-blocks made of 16 blocks of 16, with a 6-bit value per weight and an 8-bit scale per block. One FP16 scale per super-block sets the overall range.

name: GGUF Q5_K_M
bpw_note: approx.; 5.7036 measured on Llama-3.1-8B, whole-file average of a mix (Q5_K nominal 5.5)
best_for: A high-quality everyday choice when you have a little more memory than Q4_K_M needs.
how: Most tensors use Q5_K: 5-bit values with 6-bit scales and minimums for each 32-weight block inside 256-weight super-blocks. llama.cpp raises selected attention-value and feed-forward-down layers to Q6_K to protect the most sensitive weights.

name: GGUF Q5_K_S
bpw_note: approx.; 5.5704 measured on Llama-3.1-8B (Q5_K nominal 5.5)
best_for: Slightly smaller than Q5_K_M, at a small, measurable cost in quality.
how: Applies Q5_K to almost every tensor and skips the extra Q6_K upgrades that the M variant adds. The output layer still gets a higher-precision type.

name: GGUF Q4_K_M
bpw_note: approx.; 4.8944 measured on Llama-3.1-8B, whole-file average of a mix (Q4_K nominal 4.5)
best_for: The common default for local LLMs, with good quality at about 30% of FP16 size.
how: Most tensors use Q4_K: 4-bit values with 6-bit scales and minimums for each 32-weight block in a 256-weight super-block. About half of the attention-value and feed-forward-down layers, chosen by a fixed layer pattern, are stored as Q6_K instead.

name: GGUF Q4_K_S
bpw_note: approx.; 4.6672 measured on Llama-3.1-8B (Q4_K nominal 4.5)
best_for: Tighter memory budgets where Q4_K_M does not quite fit.
how: Uses Q4_K for nearly all tensors and upgrades only a few early attention-value and feed-forward-down layers to Q5_K. It is smaller than Q4_K_M because it skips most of the Q6_K upgrades.

name: GGUF Q4_0
bpw_note: nominal: 32 4-bit values + one FP16 scale = 18 bytes per 32 weights; whole-file average runs slightly higher
best_for: Maximum compatibility and simple kernels; for quality, Q4_K_M or IQ4_XS are usually better.
how: A symmetric round-to-nearest scheme. Each block of 32 weights stores 4-bit integers and one FP16 scale, with no offset, and a weight is rebuilt as integer × scale.

source.title: Hugging Face Hub docs: GGUF quantization types

name: GGUF Q3_K_M
bpw_note: approx.; 3.9960 measured on Llama-3.1-8B, whole-file average of a mix (Q3_K nominal 3.4375)
best_for: Fitting a larger model into limited RAM or VRAM when a 4-bit file will not fit.
how: Most tensors use Q3_K, which stores 3-bit values in 16-weight blocks with 6-bit scales. Attention-value, attention-output and feed-forward-down tensors are raised to Q4_K or Q5_K, which pushes the file average close to 4 bits.

name: GGUF Q3_K_S
bpw_note: approx.; 3.6429 measured on Llama-3.1-8B (Q3_K nominal 3.4375)
best_for: Very tight memory before you drop to 2-bit, with a clearly measurable quality loss.
how: Applies Q3_K to nearly every tensor and skips the higher-precision upgrades that the M and L variants use. Only special tensors such as the output layer keep a higher-precision type.

name: GGUF Q2_K
bpw_note: approx.; 3.1593 measured on Llama-3.1-8B, whole-file average of a mix (Q2_K block nominal 2.625)
best_for: Running a very large model on small hardware when a noticeable quality drop is acceptable.
how: Most weights use Q2_K, which stores 2-bit values with 4-bit scales and minimums per 16-weight block. Attention-value, attention-output and feed-forward-down tensors are kept at Q3_K or Q4_K, which is why the file averages more than 3 bits per weight.

name: GGUF IQ4_XS
bpw_note: approx.; 4.4597 measured on Llama-3.1-8B; nominal 4.25 for the IQ4_XS block
best_for: 4-bit-class quality in less memory than Q4_K_S.
how: Each weight is a 4-bit index into a fixed, non-uniform table of 16 values, so the grid is denser near zero where most weights sit. Weights are packed in 256-weight super-blocks with compact sub-block scales, and an importance matrix improves results but is not required.

name: GGUF IQ3_XXS
bpw_note: approx.; 3.2548 measured on Llama-3.1-8B; nominal 3.06 for the IQ3_XXS block
best_for: The smallest usable 3-bit-class file when you can build an importance matrix first.
how: Small groups of weights are stored as indices into a fixed 256-entry codebook grid instead of as independent values. llama.cpp refuses to produce this type without an importance matrix (imatrix).

name: GGUF IQ2_XS
bpw_note: approx.; 2.5882 measured on Llama-3.1-8B; nominal 2.31 for the IQ2_XS block
best_for: Fitting very large models into consumer memory, accepting a large quality loss.
how: Groups of eight weights are encoded as an index into a 512-entry codebook of 8-value patterns, plus sign bits and small block scales. llama.cpp requires an importance matrix for this type.

name: GGUF IQ1_S
bpw_note: approx.; 2.0042 measured on Llama-3.1-8B whole file; nominal 1.56 for the IQ1_S block (other tensors stay at higher precision)
best_for: Experiments and extreme memory limits only; on most models quality collapses.
how: Groups of weights are mapped to entries in a large codebook of patterns built from −1, 0 and +1, with a shared scale per block. llama.cpp requires an importance matrix, and on Llama-3-8B its own perplexity table shows a very large accuracy loss.

name: GPTQ 4-bit (group size 128)
bpw_note: approx., computed: 4-bit weights + one FP16 scale and one packed 4-bit zero per 128-weight group; FP16 embeddings and head add more
best_for: Fast 4-bit GPU serving of models that already ship GPTQ checkpoints.
how: Quantizes one layer at a time, using second-order (Hessian) information from a small calibration set to adjust the remaining weights so each rounding error is compensated. The paper reports quantizing a 175B model in about four GPU hours.

source.title: GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers (arXiv:2210.17323)

name: AWQ 4-bit
bpw_note: approx., computed for the common group size 128: 4-bit weights + FP16 scale and packed 4-bit zero per group
best_for: 4-bit GPU inference that generalizes well across domains, including instruction-tuned and multimodal models.
how: Uses activation statistics from calibration data to find the roughly 1% of weight channels that matter most, then scales those channels up before quantizing so they lose less precision. It needs no backpropagation; the original AutoAWQ library is archived and the method now lives in vLLM's llm-compressor.

source.title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration (arXiv:2306.00978)

name: EXL2 (variable bpw)
bpw_note: variable: any average from 2 to 8 bpw, chosen at conversion time
best_for: Hitting an exact VRAM target on a single consumer NVIDIA GPU.
how: Mixes 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8-bit quantization within and across layers, using GPTQ's optimization method and calibration error measurements to pick the combination that meets a target average bitrate. The ExLlamaV2 repo is now archived in favour of ExLlamaV3 and its EXL3 format.

name: bitsandbytes LLM.int8()
bpw_note: 8-bit weights; outlier feature columns are computed in 16-bit
best_for: Loading a model in about half its FP16 memory with no calibration step.
how: Matrix multiplications run in 8-bit with separate scaling for each row and column, while the rare outlier feature dimensions are pulled out and multiplied in 16-bit. The paper reports that more than 99.9% of values are still multiplied in 8-bit.

source.title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale (arXiv:2208.07339)

name: bitsandbytes NF4
bpw_note: approx.; 4 + 0.127 bits of constants with double quantization at block size 64 (4.5 without), per the QLoRA paper
best_for: QLoRA fine-tuning and quick 4-bit loading of Hugging Face models without calibration.
how: Each weight is snapped to one of 16 levels placed at quantiles of a normal distribution, scaled by the absolute maximum of its 64-weight block, and the levels include an exact zero. Double quantization then compresses the per-block scales themselves.

source.title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs (arXiv:2305.14314)

name: HQQ (Half-Quadratic Quantization)
bpw_note: variable: 8, 4, 3, 2 or 1-bit weights plus per-group scale and zero-point; depends on group size
best_for: Quantizing very large models in minutes when you have no calibration data.
how: Leaves the weights fixed and solves only for each group's zero-point and scale, minimizing a sparsity-promoting error (an lp norm with p below 1) with a fast closed-form half-quadratic solver. The authors report processing Llama-2-70B in under five minutes.

source.title: Half-Quadratic Quantization of Large Machine Learning Models (Dropbox HQQ blog)

name: SmoothQuant W8A8 (INT8)
bpw_note: INT8 weights and INT8 activations
best_for: Running weights and activations in INT8 on hardware with fast integer matrix units.
how: Activation outliers make activations hard to quantize, so SmoothQuant divides each activation channel by a smoothing factor and multiplies the matching weight row by the same factor, moving difficulty from activations to weights without changing the layer's output. The factors come from calibration statistics; the paper used 512 sentences and a default migration strength of 0.5.

source.title: SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for LLMs (arXiv:2211.10438)

name: FP8 E4M3
bpw_note: 1 sign, 4 exponent, 3 mantissa bits; per-tensor or finer scales add a little
best_for: Halving memory versus BF16 on GPUs with native FP8 math (NVIDIA Ada, Hopper, Blackwell).
how: An 8-bit float with more precision and less range than E5M2. Its largest normal value is 448 and it has no infinity encoding, and the FP8 paper recommends it for weights and activations; dynamic per-tensor scaling needs no calibration data.

name: FP8 E5M2
bpw_note: 1 sign, 5 exponent, 2 mantissa bits
best_for: Gradients in FP8 training; it also exists as a KV-cache dtype option in vLLM.
how: An 8-bit float that trades a mantissa bit for an extra exponent bit, reaching a maximum of 57,344 and following IEEE conventions for infinities and NaN. The FP8 paper recommends it for gradient tensors, and Transformer Engine's hybrid recipe uses it in the backward pass.

name: MXFP4
bpw_note: computed from the OCP MX v1.0 spec: 4-bit E2M1 elements + one 8-bit E8M0 scale per 32-element block
best_for: Open-weight models released natively in MXFP4, such as gpt-oss MoE weights.
how: Each block of 32 values shares one power-of-two scale (E8M0), and each element is a tiny 4-bit float (E2M1). The spec covers activations and training too, but the best-known public use is storing gpt-oss's mixture-of-experts weights.

name: MXFP8
bpw_note: computed from the OCP MX v1.0 spec: 8-bit FP8 (E4M3 or E5M2) elements + one 8-bit E8M0 scale per 32-element block
best_for: FP8 training and inference on NVIDIA Blackwell with finer-grained scaling than per-tensor FP8.
how: Gives every block of 32 FP8 values its own power-of-two scale, so one outlier only affects its own block. That lets E4M3 be used for all tensors in training rather than switching to E5M2 for gradients.

name: NVFP4
bpw_note: approx.; 4-bit E2M1 value + one FP8 E4M3 scale per 16 values, plus one FP32 scale per tensor
best_for: 4-bit inference on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with accuracy close to FP8.
how: Like MXFP4 it stores 4-bit E2M1 values, but it uses smaller 16-value blocks and an FP8 E4M3 block scale that can take non-power-of-two values, plus a per-tensor FP32 scale. For W4A4, a small calibration sample sets the per-tensor activation scale.

source.title: Introducing NVFP4 for Efficient and Accurate Low-Precision Inference (NVIDIA Technical Blog)

name: BF16 / FP16 (16-bit baseline)
bpw_note: BF16: 1 sign, 8 exponent, 7 mantissa bits; FP16: 1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 mantissa bits
best_for: The unquantized reference that every other format is measured against.
how: Most models are released in one of these 16-bit floats. BF16 keeps FP32's exponent range with less precision, while FP16 has more precision but a much narrower range.

source.title: BFloat16: The secret to high performance on Cloud TPUs (Google Cloud Blog)

name: BitNet b1.58 (ternary)
bpw_note: log2(3) ≈ 1.58 bits of information per ternary weight; packed storage varies (llama.cpp TQ1_0 1.69, TQ2_0 2.06 bpw)
best_for: Models trained from the start for ternary weights that run efficiently on CPUs.
how: Every weight is −1, 0 or +1 after scaling by the matrix's mean absolute value, and activations use 8 bits per token. The model is trained this way rather than converted afterwards, and the paper reports it matching an FP16 LLaMA baseline in perplexity from 3B parameters.

source.title: The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits (arXiv:2402.17764)

name: AQLM
bpw_note: variable by codebook scheme; typical checkpoints are labelled 2-bit (e.g. 1x16, 2x8), and 1-bit variants exist
best_for: Extreme 2-bit compression where accuracy per byte matters most.
how: Represents each small group of weights as the sum of entries from several learned codebooks (additive quantization), with the codebooks tuned jointly across each transformer block using calibration data. The authors report it is Pareto-optimal for accuracy versus size below 3 bits per parameter.

source.title: Extreme Compression of Large Language Models via Additive Quantization (arXiv:2401.06118)

name: QuIP#
bpw_note: 2, 3 or 4 bpw configurations
best_for: Research-grade quality at 2 to 4 bits per weight.
how: Applies a randomized Hadamard transform so weights look evenly spread (incoherence processing), then vector-quantizes groups of eight using a codebook built on the E8 lattice, with optional fine-tuning. Its authors have since moved on to QTIP, and the repo is no longer actively developed.

source.title: QuIP#: Even Better LLM Quantization with Hadamard Incoherence and Lattice Codebooks (arXiv:2402.04396)

name: KV cache Q8_0 (llama.cpp)
bpw_note: nominal; same Q8_0 block layout (32 int8 values + FP16 scale) applied to cached keys and values
best_for: Fitting longer context into the same memory with very little quality impact.
how: Stores attention keys and values in 8-bit blocks instead of FP16, roughly halving cache memory. In llama.cpp a quantized V cache requires Flash Attention; other allowed cache types include q4_0, q4_1, q5_0, q5_1 and iq4_nl.

name: FP8 KV cache (vLLM)
bpw_note: FP8 E4M3 or E5M2 values; scales per tensor or per attention head
best_for: Serving more tokens or longer contexts per GPU in production inference servers.
how: Keys and values are written to the cache in FP8 instead of 16-bit. Without calibration every scale defaults to 1.0, and vLLM recommends calibrating scales with llm-compressor for best accuracy.
